summary: Defines a portion of the Management Information Base for remote network monitoring. It describes objects that monitoring devices, called probes, keep so a management station can collect statistics and watch network traffic. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Some small devices sit on a network and quietly count what passes by. This describes the list of numbers they keep so a manager can read them from far away.

questions: what groups are in the rmon mib
how do rmon alarms and thresholds work
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let a management station read statistics, alarms and captured packets from a remote network probe.

tldr.problem: A network manager needs statistics, alarms and traffic detail from far-away network segments, even when the link to the management station is slow, intermittent or down.
tldr.mechanism: RMON defines a MIB module in which a probe keeps ten optional groups of tables (statistics, history, alarms, hosts, matrices, filters, packet capture, events and more) that it fills on its own and that a management station reads and configures over SNMP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2819 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 1757. It republishes the RMON MIB in SMIv2 format while remaining semantically identical to the SMIv1-based version.

today: RFC 2819 is an Internet Standard (STD 59) and has not been obsoleted. It obsoletes RFC 1757, and companion documents extend RMON to Token Ring (RFC 1513) and to application-layer analysis (RFC 2021).

sections.title: Remote Monitoring Probes and Their Goals
sections.content:
Remote network monitoring devices, often called monitors or probes, are instruments that exist to manage a network. They are often stand-alone devices, and an organization may use one per network segment. A service provider may also use them to reach a client network.

The RFC lists five goals:

  • Offline operation: the probe keeps collecting statistics even when the management station cannot reach it, and may try to notify the station about exceptional conditions.
  • Proactive monitoring: the probe runs diagnostics and logs performance so history is available when a failure starts.
  • Problem detection and reporting: the probe checks for configured conditions and can log them or notify stations.
  • Value added data: for example, highlighting the hosts that generate the most traffic or errors.
  • Multiple managers: several management stations may use the probe at once.

The objects are an interface between an RMON agent and a management application, not something meant for people to edit by hand. Some objects are Ethernet-specific; the design allows similar objects for other network types, and companion documents cover Token Ring, application-layer analysis (RMON-2) and switched networks (SMON).
sections.plainLanguage: A probe is like a lifeguard who keeps watching the pool and writing things down, even when the boss is away. When the boss comes back, the notes are ready.

sections.title: How the MIB Is Organized
sections.content:
The module is registered under rmon, which is { mib-2 16 }. Objects fall into ten groups, and the groups are the basic unit of conformance: if a probe implements a group, it must implement all objects in it. All groups are optional, but implementations must also implement the system group of MIB-II and the IF-MIB.

  • Ethernet statistics: free-running counters per monitored Ethernet interface (etherStatsTable).
  • History control and Ethernet history: periodic samples stored for later retrieval.
  • Alarm: samples a variable and compares it with thresholds. It requires the event group.
  • Host: statistics for each host discovered from MAC addresses in good packets.
  • HostTopN: reports of the hosts that top a list ordered by a rate-based statistic. It requires the host group.
  • Matrix: statistics for conversations between pairs of addresses.
  • Filter: matches packets with filter equations to form channels.
  • Packet capture: captures packets that flow through a channel. It requires the filter group.
  • Event: controls the generation of events, with an event table and a log table.

The statistics counters cover things such as octets, packets, broadcasts, multicasts, CRC and alignment errors, undersize and oversize packets, fragments, jabbers, collisions, and counts of packets in size ranges from 64 octets up to 1024 to 1518 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The probe's notebook has ten chapters: counts, history, alarms, who is talking, who talks most, who talks to whom, filters, saved packets and events. A device can keep any chapters it likes, but if it keeps a chapter it must fill in every page.

sections.title: Control Tables, Owners and Sharing
sections.content:
Many groups pair a read-write control table, where parameters are set up, with a read-only data table that holds results. Because control parameters describe the resulting data, many can only be changed while the entry is invalid. To change them, a station invalidates the control entry, which deletes it and its data, then creates a new one. This also reclaims the resources.

To let several stations share a scarce probe, each station-initiated function carries an owner label (the OwnerString type, up to 127 octets). It lets a station recognize its own resources and lets an operator find who holds a resource. A probe or administrator that sets up long-lived default functions uses an owner string starting with monitor. A station is encouraged to scan a control table for an existing entry with similar parameters before creating a new one, and should know that the owner of a shared entry may modify or delete it. The RFC notes that this only helps cooperating managers; it is not access control.

Rows are added with the method of RFC 1905. Each control entry has an EntryStatus object with the values valid(1), createRequest(2), underCreation(3) and invalid(4). If two managers try to create the same row at once, only the first succeeds and the others get an error. The agent should check parameters as each is set rather than when the entry becomes valid, so the manager learns which one was wrong.
sections.plainLanguage: Many bosses share one helper, so each one writes their name on the jobs they start. That way people can tell whose job is whose, and nobody grabs the same job number at the same time.

sections.title: Alarms, Thresholds and Events
sections.content:
The alarm group periodically samples a variable and compares it with two configured thresholds. The variable, named by alarmVariable, must resolve to an integer-like type (INTEGER, Integer32, Counter32, Counter64, Gauge or TimeTicks). The sample type is either absoluteValue, which compares the value directly, or deltaValue, which compares the change since the last sample.

A hysteresis mechanism limits alarms. One event is generated when the rising threshold is crossed upward, and no more rising events occur until the value falls back and reaches the falling threshold, and the reverse applies for the falling threshold. The alarmStartupAlarm object controls whether a first sample that is already past a threshold raises a rising alarm, a falling alarm or either.

Each alarm points to events by index. The event table says what the probe does: none, log, snmptrap or logandtrap. Logged events go into a log table, and trap events are sent to the community named in eventCommunity. Two notifications are defined, risingAlarm and fallingAlarm. An event index of zero means no event is generated.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a smoke alarm with two settings: it rings once when the smoke gets too high, and will not ring again until the air has cleared and then gotten smoky again. That keeps it from ringing nonstop.

sections.title: Hosts, Matrix, Filters and Packet Capture
sections.content:
The host group learns hosts by keeping the source and destination MAC addresses seen in good packets received promiscuously. It has a control table, a host table and a host time table. The hostTopN group builds reports of the top hosts by a chosen statistic, measured as a rate over an interval the station specifies, with the station choosing how many hosts to report. The matrix group creates a new table entry whenever it detects a new conversation between two addresses.

The filter group matches packets against filter equations. Matched packets form a data stream called a channel, which can be captured or can generate events. A filter matches packet data using an offset, a data value and masks, and also matches a packet status. For Ethernet, the status bits mark a packet longer than 1518 octets, shorter than 64 octets, or with a CRC or alignment error. The RFC's example is that an Ethernet fragment has a status value of 6.

The packet capture group stores packets that pass through a channel, with a control table and a capture buffer table. The RFC defines good packets as error-free with a valid frame length (on Ethernet, from 64 to 1518 octets), and bad packets as properly framed packets that contain errors or have an invalid length.
sections.plainLanguage: The probe can keep a list of everyone it has seen talking, find the chattiest ones, and note who talks to whom. It can also be told to look only for certain kinds of messages and keep copies of them.

sections.title: Conformance and Format
sections.content:
The module's rmonCompliance statement says that at least one of the groups must be implemented to conform to the RMON MIB, and each group is individually optional. Implementations must also implement the MIB-II system group and the IF-MIB.

RFC 2819 is written in SMIv2. A SMIv1 version can be produced by translation and must be semantically equivalent, except for objects that cannot be translated because they use Counter64. The module's revision history notes that this version reformats the module into SMIv2, while the earlier revision published as RFC 1757 made bug fixes and clarifications, including removal of the packetMatch trap.
sections.plainLanguage: A device only has to do at least one chapter of the notebook, but it must do each chapter it claims completely. The same notebook is written in a newer style here, with the same meaning.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
To work, a probe must capture all packets on its local network, including packets between third parties, and analyze them for addresses, protocol usage and conversation statistics. This data can be sensitive, so the administrator may wish to restrict SNMP access to the probe. The packet capture functions can return captured packet contents, potentially including sensitive user data or passwords, and the RFC recommends restricting SNMP access to them.

Objects with read-write or read-create access are also sensitive, since SET operations without proper protection can hurt network operations. SNMPv1 by itself is not secure. Implementors are advised to consider SNMPv3, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model, and it is the user's responsibility to configure access so only legitimate principals can read or change these objects.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe sees everyone's mail go by, so only trusted people should be allowed to ask what it saw or to change how it works.
